``` r
library(gtropic)
```

Published datasets get revised. A correction is applied, a year is added, a
column gains a better definition -- and an analysis you ran last spring no longer
reproduces. This vignette covers how `gtropic` lets you pin a retrieval exactly,
and how to manage the downloads it makes.

## Two datasets, two version numbers

The G-TROPIC collection is published as two Dataverse datasets rather than one:

- a **historical** dataset, covering 1980 up to the end of the last complete
  year, which also holds the only copy of the shared metadata (the
  administrative unit lookup, the codebook, the boundary geometries);
- a **current-year** dataset, republished as the ongoing season progresses.


``` r
gtropic_years()
#> $historical
#>  [1] 1980 1981 1982 1983 1984 1985 1986 1987 1988 1989 1990 1991 1992 1993 1994
#> [16] 1995 1996 1997 1998 1999 2000 2001 2002 2003 2004 2005 2006 2007 2008 2009
#> [31] 2010 2011 2012 2013 2014 2015 2016 2017 2018 2019 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024
#> [46] 2025
#> 
#> $current
#> [1] 2026
#> 
#> $all
#>  [1] 1980 1981 1982 1983 1984 1985 1986 1987 1988 1989 1990 1991 1992 1993 1994
#> [16] 1995 1996 1997 1998 1999 2000 2001 2002 2003 2004 2005 2006 2007 2008 2009
#> [31] 2010 2011 2012 2013 2014 2015 2016 2017 2018 2019 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024
#> [46] 2025 2026
```

You do not normally need to think about this. The package works out which
dataset holds which year by asking the server, so the annual changeover happens
without any action from you -- and without a package update. Shared metadata is
always read from the historical dataset, whatever years your query covers.

The consequence that does matter: the two datasets have **independent version
numbers**. A query spanning both is not described by any single version string,
which is why a single `version` argument would not be enough to reproduce it.

## The manifest

A **manifest** is a record of exactly which published files went into a result:
their paths, which dataset and version each came from, their sizes, and their
MD5 checksums. Every result carries one.


``` r
phl <- gtropic_data(
  WHO_ENTITY = "Philippines",
  date_range = c(2015, 2016)
)
#> Downloading 'metadata/adm2.parquet'.
#> Downloading '02_wind/storm_metadata/2015.parquet'.
#> Downloading '02_wind/storm_metadata/2016.parquet'.
#> Retrieving 14 files (256.5 MB) ; .
#> Downloading '02_wind/exposures/2015.parquet'.
#> Downloading '02_wind/exposures/2016.parquet'.
#> Downloading '02_wind/zero_pairs/2015.parquet'.
#> Downloading '02_wind/zero_pairs/2016.parquet'.
#> Downloading '04_precip/2015.parquet'.
#> Downloading '04_precip/2016.parquet'.
#> Downloading '03_flood/2015.parquet'.
#> Downloading '03_flood/2016.parquet'.
#> Downloading '01_pop/2015.parquet'.
#> Downloading '01_pop/2016.parquet'.
#> Downloading 'metadata/codebook.json'.

gtropic_manifest(phl)
#> 
#> ── gtropic version manifest ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> • Server: "demo.dataverse.org"
#> • Historical: "doi:10.70122/FK2/SWEYST" (version "3.0")
#> • Current-year: "doi:10.70122/FK2/DDSYYD" (version "4.0")
#> • Files recorded: 14
#> • Total size: 256.5 MB
#> • Retrieved: 2026-09-08 16:41:03 EDT
#> • Package version: "0.0.0.9000"
#> 
#> ℹ Pass this object as `manifest` to `gtropic_data()` to
#> reproduce the same retrieval.
```

The file-level detail is a tibble:


``` r
head(gtropic_manifest(phl)$files)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 7
#>   dataset_doi     dataset_version directory_label label file_id md5   size_bytes
#>   <chr>           <chr>           <chr>           <chr>   <int> <chr>      <dbl>
#> 1 doi:10.70122/F… 3.0             metadata        adm2… 2702301 7b85…     869564
#> 2 doi:10.70122/F… 3.0             02_wind/storm_… 2015… 2703906 9c44…       4776
#> 3 doi:10.70122/F… 3.0             02_wind/storm_… 2016… 2703907 f1b7…       4647
#> 4 doi:10.70122/F… 3.0             02_wind/exposu… 2015… 2706345 8c09…    6754848
#> 5 doi:10.70122/F… 3.0             02_wind/exposu… 2016… 2706346 562b…    7613264
#> 6 doi:10.70122/F… 3.0             02_wind/zero_p… 2015… 2706396 9aff…   49588960
```

You can see the dataset versions without digging, because `print()` on a result
shows them:


``` r
phl
#> 
#> ── G-TROPIC data ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> • Historical dataset: version "3.0"
#> • Current-year dataset: version "4.0"
#> • Genesis dates: "2015-01-01" to "2016-12-31"
#> • Storms: 129
#> • ADM2 units: 86
#> 
#> ── Tables
#> • wind: 3602 rows x 12 columns
#> • precip: 3296 rows x 3 columns
#> • flood: 789 rows x 7 columns
#> • pop: 172 rows x 6 columns
#> • storm_metadata: 129 rows x 4 columns
#> • adm2: 86 rows x 5 columns
#> • codebook: 7 entries (list)

#> 
#> ℹ Use `summary()` for detail.
```

## The reproducibility round trip

Save the manifest alongside your analysis:


``` r
mf <- gtropic_manifest(phl)
saveRDS(mf, "phl-2015-2016-manifest.rds")
```

Months later, on another machine, pass it back:


``` r
phl2 <- gtropic_data(
  WHO_ENTITY = "Philippines",
  date_range = c(2015, 2016),
  manifest = readRDS("phl-2015-2016-manifest.rds")
)
```

Exactly the files recorded in the manifest are retrieved, and their checksums
verified. `version` and the DOI options are ignored -- honouring them would
defeat the purpose.

Two failure modes are deliberate errors rather than silent substitutions:

- **A recorded file is no longer available.** You are told which one. Silently
  falling back to the current version would mean your "reproduction" quietly
  used different data.
- **A recorded file's checksum has changed.** The file at that path is not the
  file you used, whatever it is now called.

Keep the filters when you re-run. The manifest pins *which files* are read, not
which rows are selected; the filters still do their work. Supplying a manifest
alongside different filters will error if it does not contain the files those
filters need.

## Asking for a specific version

If you want a particular published version without having a manifest to hand:


``` r
# The same version string for both datasets
gtropic_data(WHO_ENTITY = "Cuba", date_range = 2019, version = "2.0")

# Different versions per dataset
gtropic_data(
  WHO_ENTITY = "Cuba",
  date_range = c(2019, 2026),
  version = c(historical = "2.0", current = "1.3")
)
```

A manifest is still the better tool for reproducibility, because it records
checksums as well as version numbers.

## Caching

A **cache** is a folder of files you have already downloaded, kept so that
repeating or extending a query does not fetch them again. It is switched off by
default: a package should not write to your disk without being asked.


``` r
gtropic_cache_enable()
```

The cache lives in the standard per-user location R reserves for package data on
your operating system:


``` r
gtropic_cache_dir()
#> [1] "/Users/lgc2035/Library/Caches/org.R-project.R/R/gtropic"
```

You can put it somewhere with more room:


``` r
gtropic_cache_enable(dir = "~/data/gtropic-cache")
```

Or enable it for a single call without changing your settings:


``` r
gtropic_data(WHO_ENTITY = "Viet Nam", date_range = 2020, cache = TRUE)
```

### What gets cached, and why it helps

The cache stores whole published year-files exactly as the repository serves
them. It never stores filtered results.

That single decision is what makes it useful. Because the unit is a year-file
rather than a query, overlapping work reuses downloads without any cleverness:

- Asking for 2001-2003, then later for 2002-2005, downloads only 2004 and 2005.
- A worldwide query, then a query for one country in a year you already have,
  downloads nothing at all -- the filtering happens locally, from files you have.

Files are stored by checksum, which deduplicates across dataset versions
automatically: a year-file that did not change between version 1.0 and version
2.0 has one checksum and is kept once, even though two versions reference it.
Checksums are verified when files are written and again when they are read, so a
corrupted file is detected and re-downloaded rather than quietly analysed.

### Managing the cache


``` r
gtropic_cache_list()    # one row per cached file
gtropic_cache_size()    # total bytes on disk
```


``` r
# Keep it under 20 GB, and drop anything older than six months
gtropic_cache_prune(max_size_gb = 20, older_than_days = 180)

# Start over
gtropic_cache_clear()

# Stop caching; keeps what is already stored
gtropic_cache_disable()
```

Pruning removes least-recently-fetched files first.

## The download guardrail

`gtropic_data()` with no arguments means roughly 47 years of global daily
rainfall. Before downloading, the package estimates the transfer -- subtracting
anything already cached -- and compares it against a threshold, one gigabyte by
default.

Under the threshold, it proceeds. Over it, in an interactive session, it tells
you the size and asks. Over it in a **non-interactive** session, such as a
scheduled job or a rendered report, it raises an error instead, naming the size
and how to proceed. Waiting forever on a prompt nobody will answer is a worse
outcome than failing immediately.

To proceed anyway:


``` r
gtropic_data(WHO_ENTITY = "India", date_range = c(1990, 2020), confirm = FALSE)
```

Or raise the threshold for the session:


``` r
options(gtropic.confirm_threshold_gb = 10)
```

Usually the better response is to narrow the query. Bear in mind that any query
including rainfall or flooding also downloads the zero-pairs files, so a
full-history rainfall query is legitimately large.

## Working with data larger than memory

By default results are ordinary data frames, held in memory. Setting
`as = "arrow"` returns them in a form that stays on disk or in a compact
in-memory representation until you ask for it.

**Arrow** is a format for holding tabular data efficiently and reading only the
columns and rows you need. In practice you use the same `dplyr` verbs, and add
`collect()` when you want ordinary data frames back:


``` r
library(dplyr)

res <- gtropic_data(
  WHO_ENTITY = "India",
  date_range = c(2000, 2010),
  as = "arrow"
)

heavy_days <- res$precip |>
  filter(PRECIP_MM > 100) |>
  group_by(ADM2_ID) |>
  summarise(days = n()) |>
  collect()
```

To be honest about the limits: genuine out-of-memory processing needs caching
switched on, because that is what puts the files on disk where they can be
streamed. Without caching, `as = "arrow"` mainly saves conversion time rather
than memory.

## Pointing at a different repository

The server and dataset identifiers are options, so moving to a different
Dataverse installation requires no package update:


``` r
options(
  gtropic.server = "dataverse.harvard.edu",
  gtropic.doi_historical = "doi:10.7910/DVN/EXAMPLE"
)
```

See `?gtropic_options` for the full list.

## What to record in a paper

At minimum: the package version, the dataset DOIs and their version numbers, and
the window and radius settings if you changed them from the defaults. All of it
is on the result:


``` r
mf <- gtropic_manifest(phl)

mf$historical_doi
mf$historical_version
mf$current_doi
mf$current_version
mf$gtropic_version

gtropic_filters(phl)[c("precip_days_before", "precip_days_after",
                       "precip_radius_km", "flood_match")]
```

Depositing the manifest itself alongside your analysis code is better still: it
lets a reader reproduce your exact inputs rather than approximate them.
